title: Mirabel and the Spire Revisited
premise: Ansel Underhill has spent her life as the gatekeeper of Hollowmere, a valley where magic cannot enter, believing her isolation protects the world from what lies beyond. When she finds tonight's date inscribed in a century-old prophecy book, she learns the valley wasn't built to keep magic out—it was built to keep her in, because she is the unacknowledged heir of the king now possessed by the entity called the Spire. Guided by the prophecy's author's ghost and a disgraced royal cartographer, Ansel must leave the only home she's known, unbind King Aldric from the thing wearing his crown, and claim an inheritance she never wanted. In the end, she refuses both crown and gate: she dissolves the Spire by accepting her dual nature as keeper and heir, then reopens the valley so magic—and belonging—can finally flow both ways.
about_author: L. M. Ishikawa is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing estate libraries in the English countryside before turning to fiction full-time. Their work blends quiet domestic detail with high fantasy stakes, exploring how inheritance shapes identity.

chapters.title: The Date That Wasn't Supposed to Exist
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. While restocking the gatehouse library, Ansel finds tomorrow's date inked into a prophecy book older than the valley itself. She dismisses it as coincidence until the ink shifts before her eyes. The beat is quiet dread—the first crack in a life built on routine.

chapters.title: What the Valley Keeps Out
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Testing the valley's boundary, Ansel discovers the ward doesn't repel magic—it recognizes her blood and seals around it. A stranger, cartographer Wren Halloway, arrives seeking the 'lost heir' and confirms the prophecy names Ansel directly. Beat: vertigo of a rewritten identity.

chapters.title: Letters from a Dead Author
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV with Wren present. The prophecy's author, Edith Vane, manifests as a ghost bound to her own book, revealing she wrote it from inside the palace a century ago. She warns that the Spire consumes kings slowly, and Aldric has little time left. Beat: reluctant alliance formed over shared guilt.

chapters.title: Leaving Hollowmere
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Crossing the threshold for the first time, Ansel experiences magic flooding back into her senses—overwhelming, beautiful, terrifying. Wren teaches her to read ley-lines on their road toward the capital. Beat: grief for the safe small life, mixed with exhilaration.

chapters.title: The City That Forgot Its King
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The capital is prosperous but hollow; citizens can't remember the king's face. Wren navigates old smuggling contacts while Ansel draws unwanted attention with her uncanny resemblance to royal portraits. Beat: paranoia tightening—someone in the court knows they've come.

chapters.title: The Thing Wearing His Crown
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Infiltrating the palace, Ansel meets King Aldric and glimpses the Spire beneath his skin—a lattice of stolen memories wearing him like a coat. It speaks to her kindly, offering her a place at its side. Beat: seduction of power, and horror at being tempted.

chapters.title: Edith's Last Chapter
chapters.summary: Edith's POV (a century earlier, interwoven with present). Edith reveals she created the Spire to preserve a dying king's mind—and it outgrew her. Her final entry names the only unbinding: an heir must willingly hold both gate and crown at once. Beat: tragic symmetry between Edith and Ansel.

chapters.title: Betrayal at the Ley-Line
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren's old employer, the Lord Protector who benefits from a hollow king, captures them, revealing he's fed the Spire subjects for years. Ansel is offered to it as the final vessel. Beat: lowest point—captured, doubting Wren, doubting herself.

chapters.title: Unbinding
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. In the throne room, Ansel chooses not to destroy the Spire but to hold it—gatekeeper and heir simultaneously—pulling Aldric's scattered self back together through shared memory. The Spire dissolves when it is finally witnessed rather than contained. Beat: climax through acceptance, not violence.

chapters.title: The Gate Stands Open
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV, epilogue-like. Aldric, restored, offers Ansel the succession; she declines, instead becoming warden of a reopened Hollowmere where magic and mortals coexist. Wren stays to map the changed valley. Final beat: belonging chosen rather than inherited.
